pages.title: CampusConnect: Campus Ride Coordination and Student Safety
pages.subtitle: NPRT630 / Diploma in ICT / Group Assignment 2026
paragraphs: Final report consolidating problem definition, system analysis, interface and database design, implementation and evaluation. Prepared against the eight-page assignment brief dated 13 February 2026; its due date is TBA. Report preparation date: 5 October 2026.

Submission status: evidence-based draft. The project owner must supply the group number, team leader, all 4–6 full names and student numbers, contribution records, confirmed forked repository URL, human-testing results and final presenter recording. No invented participants or performance measurements appear in this report.

Academic authorship: the group must review and understand the code, diagrams and analysis, cite external material, and follow the institution’s rules on assisted writing. This document is not an attestation of independent authorship.

pages.title: Executive overview and report guide
paragraphs: CampusConnect coordinates campus rides for riders, drivers, administrators and security staff. A React Native/Expo client communicates with a Spring Boot REST backend and MySQL. The project brings booking, scheduling, driver decisions, trip status, messages, history, ratings and safety alerts into a single role-based workflow.

The implementation demonstrates a broad student-project feature set. Recent owner feedback led to responsive page frames, one persistent rider navigation bar, clearer back controls and scrollable dialogs. Mocked browser checks validate navigation and selected actions without charging a card or dispatching a real security unit. Nine isolated backend unit tests and a fresh TypeScript check passed on 5 October 2026.

This is not a production assurance report. Biometric matching is not implemented by the inspected face endpoints; payment records do not settle funds; live integration and multi-user usability measurements remain outstanding. Schema drift and privileged account provisioning also need attention.

pages.title: Phase 1 — Context, problem and solution
paragraphs: The campus context is Sol Plaatje University, reflected in interface text and configuration. A rider needs a pickup, destination, driver response and a way to report a safety concern. A driver needs a manageable request queue and clear trip controls; administrators need approval and account workflows; security staff need active rides and incident evidence. Campus-wide research has not been supplied, so broader transport behaviour is a design hypothesis rather than a survey finding.

Observed workflow breakdowns [F]: the owner reported that navigation could move with page content, tablet views needed to adjust, and duplicate back buttons were confusing. On 5 October the owner also requested removal of a dollar icon beside a rand-denominated fare. These are direct project feedback, not interviews with multiple students.

Existing approach comparison: phone calls can coordinate a pickup but leave trip status across separate conversations; a group chat can share requests but does not intrinsically provide structured acceptance, scoped ratings and an incident queue; an unrelated transport platform may offer booking but requires investigation of campus membership and security integration. This is a workflow comparison, not a verified market survey. Validate these assumptions with students and campus security.

The proposed improvement is a single journey with explicit statuses and role-appropriate tasks. Success should be measured using booking time, navigation mistakes, task completion and satisfaction before and after the changes; no reduction percentage is claimed.

pages.title: UML — Use cases and booking activity
paragraphs: The use-case diagram presents the actors and their tasks inside the CampusConnect boundary. Authentication supports protected tasks. Administrative approval and security dispatch belong to different roles. The activity diagram describes a rider’s immediate-booking journey, including invalid input and unavailable-driver outcomes.
pages.note: These diagrams document intended interactions supported by the inspected routes [C]. Use-case participation does not establish production authorisation completeness. If no driver accepts, the rider must see the pending state and retain a cancellation path rather than a false completion message.

pages.title: UML — Trip states and class structure
paragraphs: Ride.RideStatus declares SCHEDULED, PENDING, ACCEPTED, ENROUTE, ARRIVED, STARTED, COMPLETED and CANCELLED. The diagram summarises the intended lifecycle, not an assertion that every controller enforces every arrow. A scheduled ride requires dispatch into the request workflow. Cancelled and completed trips remain available for history.
pages.note: The class diagram represents selected actual Java entities, controller/service boundaries and repositories. Many relationships are stored as scalar IDs rather than JPA object associations. Empty scaffold files, including PaymentService and several proposed entities, are not implemented classes in this model.

pages.title: UML sequence, architecture and technology
paragraphs: A rider request crosses the client/API/database boundary. A driver’s later acceptance changes the stored ride; the client retrieves status through polling. The diagram intentionally depicts polling rather than claiming an active WebSocket delivery path. Failure responses must remain visible to the caller.

pages.title: Phase 3 — Authentication and rider entry screens
paragraphs: The catalogue covers every screen registered in mobile/App.tsx. A panel labelled ‘SCHEMATIC’ is an explanatory mock-up based on route purpose and controls, not a captured runtime screen. ‘FIXTURE CAPTURE’ identifies an actual local web screen with synthetic data. Captures and mock-ups demonstrate interface design, not real-user evaluation.
pages.note: Landing shows branding and entry; Login handles credentials and recovery; CreateAccount collects role/contact details and onboarding steps; Legal presents terms/privacy; FaceVerification represents camera permission and selfie capture; Home supports locations and requests; History lists trips with pagination and rating access. Registration step-back is retained; redundant stack headers are suppressed.

pages.title: Phase 3 — Rider controls and driver entry screens
paragraphs: The four rider tabs share a persistent sibling navigation bar. Their page area shrinks and scrolls above the bar. Secondary screens retain one back control. Shared scrollable dialogs keep actions reachable in short landscape windows.
pages.note: ScheduleRide collects route/date/time and lists planned rides; Profile exposes editable personal details and help panels; PaymentMethods saves limited display metadata and default selection; RatingDriver submits 1–5 stars; Chat is a ride-scoped message thread; DriverDashboard shows availability and requests; ViewRideDetails offers request context, rand fare, Decline and Accept Ride. Saved-card storage is not a payment gateway.

pages.title: Phase 3 — Driver and administrative workflows
paragraphs: Driver screens organise the request-to-completion journey and separate earnings/history from the active trip. Administrative screens organise applications, users and current rides. Controls that mutate state display busy feedback; map containers resize when the page dimensions change. Reporting views are dashboard summaries and earnings; no in-app downloadable report-generation screen is evidenced.
pages.note: DriverActiveRide exposes trip phases, contact, messages and cancellation; DriverEarnings aggregates completed trips; DriverHistory lists prior rides; DriverProfile presents account/vehicle details; AdminDashboard offers applications and quick actions; UserManagement filters and changes account status; RideMonitoring selects current rides for the map. Aggregated earnings are not confirmation of settlement.

pages.title: Phase 3 — Safety screens and design iterations
paragraphs: Security views prioritise ride context and incident evidence. Incident and resolved-SOS pagination reserve room instead of covering the list. A populated active-SOS list scrolls above its navigation bar. Audio playback and download errors appear as visible feedback.

paragraphs: Schema control method: inventory entity mappings and SQL migrations; compare against a disposable database; select one migration history; apply it to an empty database; inspect keys/types; execute registration, trip, chat, SOS and payment tests. Do not run fix_rides_table.sql against valuable data: it contains destructive table rebuilding.

MySQL fits relational account/trip records and reporting, while InnoDB supports transactions and referential constraints [R4]. This does not remove the need for correctly declared constraints, tested migrations, backups and least-privilege credentials. No Oracle or NoSQL benchmark was performed.

pages.title: Phase 4 — Implementation and error handling
paragraphs: The client uses registered role routes, Axios API access and shared UI components. AppLayout bounds the navigator, supplies safe-area padding and renders the rider navigation as a sibling. ScrollableCard and ConfirmationDialog keep actions reachable. screenChrome suppresses duplicate native headers where the screen already owns its controls.

The backend exposes authentication, user, driver, ride, message, payment, administrator and security controllers. JPA handles core entities; JdbcTemplate handles saved payment display records, settings and some reporting. This mixed approach makes schema consistency important. Several empty scaffold services/controllers remain and should not be counted as delivered features.

Authentication uses BCrypt and JWT; admin/security paths have role restrictions in SecurityConfig. Password reset stores a hash, expires after ten minutes, uses a five-attempt limit and a sixty-second resend cooldown. Unknown-account requests return without revealing an account. These isolated behaviours are unit-tested; SMTP delivery still needs configuration and live verification.

pages.title: Testing methods, results and colour contrast
paragraphs: Fresh verification on 5 October 2026: npm.cmd run typecheck exited successfully. mvn.cmd -o -Dtest=AuthServiceTest,PasswordResetServiceTest test compiled the project and passed nine tests with zero failures/errors/skips. Repositories and email are mocked in these tests; they do not establish database or SMTP correctness.

Session evidence from 4 October: check-responsive.cjs passed 28 rider tab/size checks, driver/security/admin layout checks, auth forms and dialogs. check-pages.cjs passed seven-size checks for detail pages and mocked card, settings, audio, security, chat and driver-trip actions. Production web export also passed. These are historical recorded checks; they are not newly measured performance or human studies.

Existing historical Surefire reports include one failure in AdminControllerPendingDriversTest (3 tests, 1 failure). Other stored controller reports are not a substitute for a fresh complete run. Some integration tests create accounts, so only the isolated services were rerun for this documentation review.

pages.note: Ratios are calculated from theme tokens using relative luminance; they do not constitute a complete accessibility audit. In particular, white text on green buttons needs a darker background or different foreground. The report therefore does not claim WCAG conformance. Test keyboard access, screen-reader labels, zoom, native touch and image text separately.

pages.title: Human evaluation: protocol and evidence gaps
paragraphs: The brief requires multiple real users, completion times, error rates and satisfaction. No completed participant dataset was supplied. Direct owner requests provide useful formative feedback, but they do not establish a multi-user study or justify numerical usability improvements. This page specifies a reproducible evaluation the group can conduct.

Recruit at least six consenting participants, including rider and driver tasks and an administrator/security reviewer where available. Use anonymous IDs rather than student numbers in results. Explain the test purpose, obtain consent, avoid live emergency dispatch and real card data, and allow participants to withdraw. Report who participated by role without identifying them.

For each task, define the start cue and successful end state before testing. Record seconds, completion without assistance, wrong taps, validation errors, help requests, device/viewport and a 1–5 ease rating. Use equivalent synthetic scenarios for a baseline and revised build, alternate test order when possible, and acknowledge learning effects. Do not invent a baseline if the earlier version is unavailable.

Compute completion rate = unaided successes / attempts; error rate = defined error events / attempts; report median task time with sample size and spread. Satisfaction averages are optional and must show raw counts. RESULTS: PENDING. Attach anonymised logs, feedback themes and actual before/after evidence.

pages.title: Execution, demonstration and delivery
paragraphs: Execution documentation accompanies the report. Install the project’s declared Java 25 and Node dependencies; provide a compatible MySQL database; configure environment secrets locally. The repository uses development ddl-auto update and schema repair, so a clean deployment must verify the schema rather than assume all historical scripts can be run in sequence. Never include real credentials, .env files or local dependency caches in submission.

Run the backend with Maven from backend and the Expo client from mobile. API port is 8080; select a free Expo port such as 8083. ApiClient uses emulator/browser defaults; a physical phone must use a reachable LAN host. Password-reset mail has a separate documented local launcher. A browser build does not prove native camera, microphone or file sharing.

The demonstration script follows a complete user journey: explain the problem → register/login → request/schedule → driver decision → message and trip status → history/rating → admin settings/users → security incident/audio → responsive navigation → limitations and technical decisions. Record the actual integrated system with test accounts for the final presentation. Include presenters’ names and be ready to explain code and answer supervisor questions.

Submission follows the discovered template: Code, Demo, Dox and a names text file, in a module/year/group/leader folder. A code archive is excluded from this working package until it can be exported without secrets/generated caches and tied to the confirmed fork. Code/README gives explicit export instructions. The repository requirement is not fulfilled merely by an existing local git folder.

pages.note: Reflection for group review: navigation stability matters because people form spatial expectations; duplicate controls create uncertainty; error messages need an action users can take. Confirm these observations in testing. Add each member’s own account of what surprised them, decisions they made and what they would change.

pages.title: Limitations, conclusion and references
paragraphs: CampusConnect demonstrates the planned campus workflow through role-specific interfaces and backend routes. Its strongest verified evidence is repeatable layout/action fixtures and isolated account/reset tests. The next priority is an integrated, disposable-database demonstration and an honest human evaluation, followed by native-device checks.

Prioritise: (1) restrict privileged registration and remove credential resets; redact sensitive account fields; (2) consolidate and test schema migrations, including payments; (3) replace selfie acceptance with real verification only if ethically approved and technically validated; (4) enforce lifecycle/assignment concurrency and evaluate external dependencies; (5) improve text contrast, keyboard access and native permissions; (6) measure real-user outcomes and record a narrated demonstration. No payment settlement, biometric assurance, campus-wide adoption, uptime or guaranteed emergency response is claimed.

This report is ready for group review but must not be described as submission-complete while names, fork identity, contribution evidence, participant results and the final demo are missing. The verified template structure is used; update folder/file names once the group number and leader are confirmed.
